# Autoresearch for behavior prediction: what 96 automated training runs taught us

To accelerate research, a lab needs to automate the choice and execution of the next experiment, not just the writing of reports. Karpathy's Autoresearch illustrates this with a small set of files, a fixed evaluation harness, and an iterative keep-or-discard rule. We implemented a bounded adaptation on actual purchase-session data, ran 96 model fits, repeated all of them, and independently recalculated the selected models' test loss.

![Experiment overview](/assets/research/ac04-cover.svg)

## The original pattern

The [official repository, pinned revision](https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch/tree/228791fb499afffb54b46200aca536f79142f117) separates program.md (research instructions), train.py (the editable training code), and prepare.py (fixed data preparation and evaluation). Each experiment uses a 300-second training budget; changes are kept when validation bits per byte improve. The separation matters because a researcher must not redefine the score to make a candidate look better.

An [existing Apple Silicon MLX port](https://github.com/trevin-creator/autoresearch-mlx/tree/766a25ff22afa799efd8d0aa450a4348e4749df2) was inspected. Our Mac had MLX, but lacked pyarrow and rustbpe and had about 1.1 GiB of free disk. We did not execute the native 300-second language-model training. The upstream README states MIT, but the pinned root LICENSE was unavailable and its GitHub API license metadata was null; the MLX fork includes an MIT license. We did not copy upstream code into this experiment. Our implementation independently follows the published research pattern.

## A real behavior-prediction task

We used the [UCI Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/468/online) (Sakar & Kastro, 2018; DOI 10.24432/C5F88Q; CC BY 4.0). It contains 12,330 sessions with purchase outcomes. We retained only six page-count and duration features for administrative, informational and product-related pages. PageValues, session-end rates, region and device fields were excluded. These are still session-level observations, not a demonstration of prospective prediction during a visit or causal intervention.

Exact duplicate feature vectors were grouped and assigned to partitions using a frozen SHA-256 rule. There were 11,312 distinct groups, with 7,604 training rows (1,160 purchases), 2,310 validation rows (359), and 2,416 test rows (389). Log-transformed feature standardization used training statistics only. This is not a chronological split.

![Search and evaluation separation](/assets/research/ac04-method.svg)

Our logistic regression minimizes binary negative log likelihood with L2 regularization. The grid crosses four learning rates (0.003, 0.03, 0.3, 3) and four regularization values (0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1). Each policy begins with the same baseline and evaluates eight distinct candidates, using exactly 80 full-batch gradient updates per fit. Hill-climbing samples an unseen neighbor of the incumbent, with a random fallback when neighbors are exhausted. Random search samples uniformly from unseen candidates. Only a validation improvement greater than 1e-12 is accepted. Six paired search seeds yield 96 fits. All selected configurations and weights are saved before a separate test-evaluation command. This is procedural separation, not a security-sealed test environment.

## Results

![Measured NLL comparison](/assets/research/ac04-results.svg)

| Policy | Validation NLL | Test NLL |
|---|---:|---:|
| Training prior | not computed | 0.441613 |
| Hill-climbing | 0.417044 | 0.424436 |
| Random search | 0.417029 | 0.424932 |

Hill-climbing improves test NLL by about 3.89% relative to the training prior. Its advantage over random search is just 0.000496 NLL, with three wins, one tie, and two losses across six paired seeds. Random search has marginally better mean validation NLL. These seeds vary the search on one dataset, not six independent datasets; neither general superiority nor a statistically established advantage follows.

The first execution completed 7,680 gradient updates; replay repeated all of them. Results match except timing and the hash that includes timing. An independent standard-library calculation recovered all twelve selected-model test losses within 1e-12. Seven unit tests pass in ordinary and optimized Python. All discarded candidates remain in the receipt with configurations, validation metrics, decisions and weights.

## From bounded automation to research infrastructure

The finite loop performs candidate selection, learning, evaluation, retention and stopping without further human input during execution. It does not generate new scientific hypotheses or arbitrary code; the search space was predefined. No Manager weights were trained, no app release was made, and no business impact or human benefit was measured.

Adopting it in Anicca's existing scheduled research process requires an independently reviewed evaluator, bounded resources, external tests and actual cost telemetry. It should not be given permission to change its own acceptance criteria or expand its budget. The native upstream run and adoption gates are tracked in [issue #819](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/819).

Data attribution: Sakar, C. & Kastro, Y. (2018), Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset, UCI Machine Learning Repository, CC BY 4.0. Adapted by Anicca through feature selection, splitting and modeling; no endorsement implied.
